literal: Hui, courtesy name Yuanxu, in youth was as famed as Xin and was also skilled in many arts.
idiomatic: Hui, style Yuanxu, rivaled Xin in youth and mastered many arts besides.

literal: He died as Attendant of the Palace Secretariat and was posthumously made Governor of Yanzhou.
idiomatic: He died as Attendant of the Palace Secretariat and was posthumously Governor of Yanzhou.

literal: Zhao, courtesy name Zhongliang, in youth loved Confucian studies and also prided himself somewhat on martial skill.
idiomatic: Zhao, style Zhongliang, cherished the classics and fancied himself no mean hand with arms.

literal: By nature he was sincere and thick and was famed for brotherly affection.
idiomatic: He was warm and steadfast, renowned for devotion to his brothers.

literal: He died as Director of Merit.
idiomatic: He died as Director of Merit.

literal: Xi, courtesy name Shulang, childhood name Shamini.
idiomatic: Xi, style Shulang, childhood name Shamini.

literal: From childhood he was filial and careful, refined and of great capacity.
idiomatic: Even as a boy he was filial, careful, elegant, and far-seeing.

literal: He loved learning and never wearied.
idiomatic: He studied without tiring.

literal: His appearance was beautiful and he had bearing.
idiomatic: He was handsome and carried himself with grace.

literal: At the end of Wei he followed his mother and elder brother east to the sea's edge and associated with Xing Ziliang.
idiomatic: When Wei foundered he went east with his mother and brother and kept company with Xing Ziliang.

literal: Ziliang loved his clarity and, writing to Xi's two elder brothers in Luoyang, said, "Your worthy younger brother Milang's mind is deep and his reach far; he is free and unbound.
idiomatic: Ziliang prized his clarity and wrote to the brothers in Luoyang, "Milang's mind runs deep and wide; he is untrammeled.

literal: Brief in haste, his words always hit principle.
idiomatic: Even rushed, his speech struck truth.

literal: When he chants feeling and nature, he is the finest of his age.
idiomatic: In poetry of the heart he has no peer.

literal: I fear you below will find it hard to be elder brothers and will have no leisure to worry that he does not advance."
idiomatic: You may struggle to play elder brother—you will not need to fret that he fails to rise."

literal: In the first year of Yong'an of Wei, his second elder brother Hui was betrothed in Liang; he had Xi released from common dress and made him Token Attendant Cavalier outside the regular rolls, and he was summoned to the staff of the Prince of Guangping as Recorder.
idiomatic: In Wei Yong'an's first year, when Hui was betrothed in Liang, Xi was given Token Attendant Cavalier and summoned to the Prince of Guangping's staff as Recorder.

literal: Xi wished to nurse his mother and in the end did not accept the appointment.
idiomatic: Xi wanted to care for his mother and declined.

literal: After his mother died, as the court moved to Ye, he wandered between Gong and Luoyang, delighting in their hills and waters.
idiomatic: After her death, when the court shifted to Ye, he roamed between Gong and Luoyang, in love with landscape.

literal: He joined Lu Yuanming of Fanyang and Wei Jijing of Julu in sworn friendship and went to Tianling Mountain, with a vast longing to end his days there.
idiomatic: With Lu Yuanming of Fanyang and Wei Jijing of Julu he swore fellowship and climbed Tianling, resolved to finish life there.

literal: When the Western Wei general Dugu Xin entered Luoyang, Xi was appointed Recorder on his staff.
idiomatic: When Dugu Xin of Western Wei took Luoyang, Xi was named Recorder on his staff.

literal: Xi claimed he had earlier been bitten by a dog and was gravely ill, and did not attend.
idiomatic: Xi said an old dog bite had laid him low, and he did not go.

literal: An old friend doubted the wound was not rabid and wrote urging him to come.
idiomatic: A friend doubted it was mad-dog fever and wrote urging him to report.

literal: Xi replied, "I am shamed by your care in asking me to rise from illness.
idiomatic: Xi answered, "Your concern shames me—you bid me rise though ill.

literal: Following through on your gracious intent, it seems you doubt that my wound may not be rabies.
idiomatic: Reading your kindness, you seem unsure this is rabies at all.

literal: Do I wish it must be rabies?
idiomatic: Do I want it to be rabies?

literal: But reason and circumstance leave no doubt.
idiomatic: Reason leaves none.

literal: As for your doubt, there is also excess in it.
idiomatic: Your doubt overshoots.

literal: Since you doubt it is not rabies, you may also doubt it is rabies—the doubt is already half.
idiomatic: Doubt it is not, and you may doubt it is—your doubt is already half the whole.

literal: If you doubt it is rabies and still nurse it, though it is not rabies there is no harm.
idiomatic: If you fear rabies and treat it, no harm comes when it is not.

literal: If you doubt it is not rabies and do not treat it, perchance it is rabies and then it cannot be saved.
idiomatic: If you deem it harmless and withhold care, and it is rabies, nothing will save you.

literal: Thus overtreatment brings ten thousand certainties of safety; overt neglect may lead to death.
idiomatic: Over-care buys perfect safety; under-care buys death.

literal: If Wang Xi were not worth keeping, then he is not worth taking;
idiomatic: If Wang Xi is worthless, do not take him;

literal: since you have taken him, he is worth keeping.
idiomatic: having taken him, he is worth keeping.

literal: How can you rob him of perfect safety and leave him to possible death!
idiomatic: Why steal his safety and risk his death!

literal: Moreover the general's authority and virtue sweep like storm and mist, about to cover the eight directions—how much less one man!
idiomatic: Your general's might rolls like wind and fog over the realm—what is one man!

literal: If you must begin with Kuai, first you must save the living.
idiomatic: If service starts with the lowly, save lives first.

literal: Why will you not speak to the general at ease on his behalf?"
idiomatic: Will you not plead for him, gently, to the general?"

literal: Only then was he granted leniency.
idiomatic: Leniency followed.

literal: Before long Xin returned, and Xi went back to Ye.
idiomatic: Soon Xin withdrew, and Xi returned to Ye.

literal: Gao Huan sought court youths who were loyal, filial, and careful to roam with his sons.
idiomatic: Gao Huan sought young men of loyalty and filial care to companion his sons.

literal: Xi, together with Cui Zhan of Qinghe, Li Du of Dunqiu, and Lu Zhengtong of Fanyang, were the first chosen.
idiomatic: Xi, with Cui Zhan, Li Du, and Lu Zhengtong, were first picked.

literal: When Wen Xiang was Grand General he took Xi's hand and said, "My younger brothers are still growing; their wills are unsettled—near goodness or near evil, they cannot but be shifted.
idiomatic: Wen Xiang as Grand General clasped their hands: "My brothers are still forming; good and ill companions will move them.

literal: You do not fail righteousness; your rank and stipend shall always stand below my brothers'—
idiomatic: Hold to righteousness; your honors shall stay beneath my brothers'—

literal: but if you knowingly lead them astray and bring mutual ruin, the guilt reaches your clan, not you alone."
idiomatic: yet if you bend them to evil, the house pays, not you alone."

literal: Xi followed Shenwu to Jinyang and was made Staff Officer in the inner and outer offices, attending Prince of Changshan Yan as friend.
idiomatic: Xi followed Shenwu to Jinyang as staff officer, companion to Prince of Changshan Yan.

literal: At the opening of Qi Tianbao he acted for Taiyuan commandery.
idiomatic: At Qi Tianbao's start he governed Taiyuan in commission.

literal: When Wenxuan grew dissolute, the Prince of Changshan remonstrated repeatedly.
idiomatic: When Wenxuan turned reckless, Prince Yan remonstrated again and again.

literal: The emperor suspected the prince borrowed words from Xi and meant to impose the death penalty.
idiomatic: The emperor thought Yan spoke through Xi and prepared capital punishment.

literal: The prince told Xi privately, "Doctor, tomorrow you must do one thing—for I mean to keep you alive and also save myself; understand deeply and do not resent it."
idiomatic: Yan whispered to Xi, "Doctor, tomorrow do a thing—to save you and me; do not blame me."

literal: Then before the assembly he beat Xi twenty strokes.
idiomatic: Before the court he had Xi thrashed twenty blows.

literal: The emperor soon raged again; hearing Xi had been beaten, for that reason he did not kill him, but shaved his head, flogged him, fettered him, and sent him to the armor workshop.
idiomatic: Wenxuan raged anew; learning Xi had been beaten, he spared his life but shaved, lashed, chained, and sent him to the armory.

literal: After three years the prince again remonstrated fiercely, was himself beaten savagely, closed his mouth and would not eat.
idiomatic: Three years on, Yan remonstrated once more, was thrashed himself, and fasted.

literal: The empress dowager was deeply grieved.
idiomatic: The empress dowager grieved.

literal: The emperor told those beside him, "If the boy dies, what of my old mother!"
idiomatic: The emperor muttered, "If the boy dies, what becomes of my mother?"

literal: Thereafter he often inquired after the prince's illness and said, "Force yourself to eat—I will give Wang Xi back to you."
idiomatic: He asked after Yan's health and said, "Eat—I will return Wang Xi."

literal: Then he released Xi and sent him to the prince.
idiomatic: Xi was freed and sent to Yan.

literal: The prince embraced Xi and said;
idiomatic: Yan embraced Xi and said:

literal: "My breath is faint—I fear we shall not meet again!"
idiomatic: "I can barely breathe—we may not meet again!"

literal: Xi wept and said, "Heaven's way and the spirits—how could they let Your Highness die in this house!"
idiomatic: Xi wept, "Heaven would not let Your Highness perish here!"

literal: "The Supreme One is elder brother to men and lord to the realm—how can one reckon with him?"
idiomatic: "The Son of Heaven is brother and sovereign—do not measure him as an equal."

literal: "If Your Highness will not eat, the empress dowager also will not eat; if Your Highness does not cherish yourself, will you not cherish her?"
idiomatic: "If you refuse food, your mother refuses it too; spare yourself for her sake."

literal: Before he finished speaking the prince forced himself to sit and eat.
idiomatic: Yan sat up and ate before Xi finished.

literal: Xi was thus spared penal service and returned as the prince's friend.
idiomatic: Xi was freed from labor and again Yan's companion.

literal: The prince again held charge of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Yan again directed the Masters of Writing.

literal: Newly appointed officers had to visit the prince to thank him for office and take leave when departing.
idiomatic: Every new appointee thanked Yan in person on taking and leaving office.

literal: Xi said to the prince, "To receive rank from the court and bow in thanks at a private house has always been reckoned a breach of discipline.
idiomatic: Xi told him, "Rank from the throne, thanks in a private house—that has always been corruption.

literal: Court civil and military, coming and going with farewells of thanks—let it all be stopped at once.
idiomatic: Let every officer's comings and goings end with one rule.

literal: The sovereign is stern in bearing; he relies on Your Highness to support him."
idiomatic: The throne stands uneasy; it leans on you."

literal: The prince took it deeply to heart.
idiomatic: Yan took the counsel to heart.

literal: He often said calmly to Xi, "The sovereign's conduct is inconstant; what your eyes and ears have gathered—can I fall silent after one burst of anger?"
idiomatic: He often told Xi, "The emperor's ways shift—what you've seen—shall I bite my tongue after one rage?"

literal: "You should draft remonstrances; I shall seize a moment to speak to the limit."
idiomatic: "Draft protests; I'll speak when the moment comes."

literal: Xi then set out more than ten items and presented them, and urgently admonished the prince, "The court is now thus—do you wish to imitate Jie Zi's common man and lightly throw away a morning's life? Madness makes a man unaware of himself; do blades and arrows know kinship?
idiomatic: Xi listed ten points and warned, "The court is mad—will you mimic Jie Zi and toss one dawn's life away? Drunken rage forgets kin; steel knows no family.

literal: Once calamity comes outside reason, what of Your Highness's house?
idiomatic: When disaster strikes beyond sense, what of your line?

literal: What of the empress dowager?
idiomatic: What of your mother?

literal: I beg you for now to yield and be cautious day by day."
idiomatic: Yield now; guard each day."

literal: The prince sobbed uncontrollably and said, "It has come to this!"
idiomatic: Yan wept, "So far gone!"

literal: The next day he saw Xi and said, "I brooded nine nights—now my mind rests."
idiomatic: Next day he said, "Nine nights I thought—now I am at peace."

literal: He ordered a fire and burned the drafts before Xi.
idiomatic: He burned the drafts before Xi.

literal: Later the prince seized chances to remonstrate bitterly and thus offended the throne.
idiomatic: Later Yan remonstrated hard and provoked wrath.

literal: The emperor had brawny men twist his arms behind him, set a white blade at his throat, and curse, "Boy, what do you know—do you mean to judge me with clerk's talent?
idiomatic: Brawlers bent his arms back, a blade at his throat: "Pup, what do you know—measuring me with clerk's skill?

literal: Who taught you?"
idiomatic: Who taught you?"

literal: The prince said, "The realm is mute—apart from me, who dares speak?"
idiomatic: Yan said, "All China is silent—who but me?"

literal: The emperor pressed for beating; he was clubbed dozens of times in confusion.
idiomatic: Wenxuan ordered blows; dozens of strokes fell at random.

literal: He was spared when the emperor fell drunk asleep.
idiomatic: Drunken sleep ended it.

literal: Afterward licentious pleasures spread through the imperial kin; wherever he lingered, he turned night into day;
idiomatic: Then debauchery ran through the clan; wherever he stayed, night became day;

literal: only at the Prince of Changshan's residence did he mostly find nothing to his liking and leave.
idiomatic: only Changshan's hall rarely pleased him long.

literal: When the emperor died, Jinan succeeded.
idiomatic: At Wenxuan's death Jinan reigned.

literal: The prince told Xi, "One man holds his hands in his sleeves—we too shall keep ease and leisure."
idiomatic: Yan told Xi, "One man reigns at ease—we too may rest."

literal: He also said, "The court is broad, benevolent, and forgiving—a true ruler who guards the laws."
idiomatic: He added, "The throne is mild and forgiving—a keeper of the old ways."

literal: Xi said, "Tianbao enjoyed the mandate, yet the eastern palace was left to a barbarian.
idiomatic: Xi said, "Tianbao held heaven's trust, yet the heir was a barbarian.

literal: Now he suddenly holds the myriad reins and drives fierce heroes.
idiomatic: Now he grips every rein and rides fierce men.

literal: If sagely virtue is still young and cannot bear twin burdens, yet another surname handles edicts in and out, power must settle somewhere.
idiomatic: If the sage is young and cannot bear double weight, yet aliens issue orders, power will find a seat.

literal: Though Your Highness wishes to keep only your fief, is that possible?
idiomatic: Though you mean to keep your fief alone, can you?

literal: Even if you could truly yield and withdraw, do you judge that your house could long keep its fortune?
idiomatic: Even yielding, do you think your line would endure?"

literal: The prince was silent, brooded long, and said, "What is to be done with me?"
idiomatic: Yan was silent, then said, "What am I to do?"

literal: Xi said, "The Duke of Zhou held King Cheng and faced the feudal lords, ruled as regent seven years, then returned the bright mandate to the son.
idiomatic: Xi said, "The Duke of Zhou held the boy-king, ruled seven years, then returned the realm.

literal: Fortunately there is this precedent—only Your Highness must ponder it."
idiomatic: The precedent exists—ponder it."

literal: The prince said, "How would I dare compare myself to the Duke of Zhou?"
idiomatic: Yan said, "How dare I match the Duke of Zhou?"

literal: Xi said, "With Your Highness's standing today, do you think you can avoid the Duke of Zhou?"
idiomatic: Xi said, "At your height today, can you avoid him?"

literal: The prince did not answer.
idiomatic: Yan said nothing.

literal: When the emperor set out, he ordered the prince to follow the carriage and made Xi chief administrator of Bing.
idiomatic: On the emperor's departure he commanded Yan to accompany him and made Xi chief administrator of Bing.
